source_user: What assumptions must be stated before making a performance claim about decode? Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Decode generates one or a few tokens per step and repeatedly reads model weights and KV state; it is often sensitive to memory bandwidth and scheduling.
corrected_answer:
Assumptions frame: single-node or 2-node A30-class serving (24 GB HBM2, ~933 GB/s theoretical HBM bandwidth, no NVLink between A30 pairs on this host, PCIe Gen4 x16 ~25 GB/s effective host-device), dense ~9B decoder in bf16 (~18 GB weights), paged KV cache, continuous batching.

Assumptions that must be stated before any decode performance claim (variant: throughput claims).

1. Workload shape. Mean and p95 input length, mean and p95 output length, and the arrival process (closed-loop N concurrent clients vs open-loop Poisson at R req/s). "1200 tok/s" is meaningless without these: at 128-token prompts and 1024-token outputs the run is decode-dominated, at 8k prompts and 64-token outputs it is prefill-dominated and the number mostly measures prefill.
2. Batching regime. Static batch vs continuous batching, max_num_seqs, max_num_batched_tokens, and whether chunked prefill is on. Chunked prefill interleaves prefill chunks into decode steps, which raises aggregate tok/s while degrading inter-token latency (ITL); a throughput claim that hides this is not comparable.
3. Metric definition. Output-only tok/s vs total (prompt+output) tok/s differ by the prompt/output ratio; report TTFT, ITL p50/p99, and end-to-end p99 alongside, or the claim is unfalsifiable.
4. Precision and KV dtype. bf16 vs fp8 weights vs AWQ/GPTQ int4, and fp16 vs fp8 KV. Note A30 is Ampere: it has no hardware fp8 path, so an fp8 result from an H100 blog does not transfer.
5. Sampling config. Greedy vs temperature/top-p, and especially speculative decoding: acceptance rate is workload dependent, so a spec-dec speedup measured on one prompt distribution is not portable.

Concrete mechanism. The decode step reads the full weight set once per step irrespective of batch size. 18 GB at an achieved ~650 GB/s (~70% of peak) is ~28 ms/step floor, i.e. ~36 tok/s/sequence, and per-GPU aggregate throughput grows nearly linearly in batch size until KV traffic per step approaches weight bytes. Therefore any tok/s claim is really a claim about the achieved batch size, which is set by KV cache capacity, not by the kernel.

Boundary condition. The linear-in-batch region ends when B * per_token_KV_bytes_read approaches the 18 GB weight read. With 40 layers, 8 KV heads, head_dim 128, bf16, per-token KV is 2*8*128*2*40 = ~1.6 MB; at context 4k a sequence holds ~6.4 GB, so on a 24 GB card only ~1 sequence at that length fits after weights. The regime therefore flips from weight-bound to KV-bound at very modest concurrency, and the claim must state the context length it was measured at.

Falsifiable prediction. Sweep B in {1,2,4,8,16} at fixed 512-in/512-out; per-step latency should stay within ~15% of the B=1 value until KV bytes/step reach roughly 30-50% of weight bytes, then rise superlinearly as preemption starts.

Evidence to demand. Server launch flags, engine and CUDA/driver versions, the benchmark harness command, raw per-request latency traces (not just means), nvidia-smi dmon or DCGM utilization/HBM-bandwidth samples, and the scheduler's preemption and cache-hit counters.

Rollback gate. If a config change does not improve p99 end-to-end latency at the target QPS by >=10% across three independent runs, or if preemption count is nonzero at steady state, revert to the previous config.

source_user: What assumptions must be stated before making a performance claim about decode? Case variant 2: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Decode generates one or a few tokens per step and repeatedly reads model weights and KV state; it is often sensitive to memory bandwidth and scheduling.
corrected_answer:
Assumptions frame: single-node or 2-node A30-class serving (24 GB HBM2, ~933 GB/s theoretical HBM bandwidth, no NVLink between A30 pairs on this host, PCIe Gen4 x16 ~25 GB/s effective host-device), dense ~9B decoder in bf16 (~18 GB weights), paged KV cache, continuous batching.

Assumptions that must be stated before any decode performance claim (variant: latency claims).

1. Which latency. TTFT (prefill + queueing) and ITL (per decode step) have different bottlenecks; a single "latency" number conflates them. Report TTFT p50/p99 and ITL p50/p99 separately, plus queue wait, because at load the dominant term is usually queueing, not kernel time.
2. Load point. Latency is only meaningful with the offered load stated. p99 ITL at 1 req/s and at 20 req/s are different physical regimes; a latency claim without the QPS and the concurrency is not reproducible.
3. Interference from prefill. With continuous batching, an arriving long prompt runs prefill in the same step stream as decode and stalls every in-flight decoder. Whether chunked prefill is enabled, and the chunk size, must be stated, since it converts one large ITL spike into many small ones.
4. Isolation. MPS/MIG mode, other tenants on the GPU, CPU pinning, and whether the tokenizer/detokenizer runs on the critical path. Detokenization and HTTP/SSE overhead can add milliseconds per token that are invisible to GPU profilers.
5. Warmup and measurement window. CUDA graphs capture, autotuning, and page-cache warmth mean the first N requests are unrepresentative; state the discard window.

Concrete mechanism. Per decode step the engine reads ~18 GB of weights plus B * ~1.6 MB * context_len of KV. At ~650 GB/s achieved, the weight term alone is ~28 ms; ITL cannot go below that on a single A30 for a dense 9B in bf16. Tensor parallelism across 2 GPUs halves the per-GPU weight read to ~9 GB (~14 ms) but adds two all-reduces per layer; over PCIe Gen4 without NVLink, an all-reduce of hidden_size*B*2 bytes at 40 layers * 2 = 80 collectives per step frequently costs more than the compute saved.

Boundary condition. TP scaling for decode is profitable only while collective time per step is small relative to the weight-read time saved. On a PCIe-only A30 pair with small B, this condition typically fails: TP=2 can be slower than TP=1. State the interconnect topology (nvidia-smi topo -m) or the claim is not interpretable.

Falsifiable prediction. On this host, TP=2 decode at B<=4 will show ITL within 20% of, or worse than, TP=1, and NCCL all-reduce time will be a visible fraction of step time in an Nsight Systems timeline.

Evidence to demand. nvidia-smi topo -m, NCCL_DEBUG=INFO ring/tree topology dump, Nsight Systems trace covering >=100 decode steps, per-request timestamped logs, and the exact client harness.

Rollback gate. If p99 ITL regresses beyond the SLO (for example 60 ms) for more than 5 consecutive minutes after a config change, roll back automatically and keep the previous engine process draining rather than killed.

corrected_answer:
Assumptions frame: single-node or 2-node A30-class serving (24 GB HBM2, ~933 GB/s theoretical HBM bandwidth, no NVLink between A30 pairs on this host, PCIe Gen4 x16 ~25 GB/s effective host-device), dense ~9B decoder in bf16 (~18 GB weights), paged KV cache, continuous batching.

Assumptions that must be stated before any decode performance claim (variant: memory and capacity claims).

1. KV cache accounting. Layers, KV heads (GQA/MQA factor), head_dim, KV dtype, block size, and the fraction of HBM given to the cache (gpu_memory_utilization). Per-token KV for 40 layers, 8 KV heads, head_dim 128, bf16 is 2*8*128*2*40 = ~1.6 MB; at 24 GB total minus ~18 GB weights minus activation and fragmentation overhead, usable KV is often <4 GB, i.e. roughly 2500 tokens total across all sequences. Any concurrency claim must be checked against this arithmetic first.
2. Fragmentation and preemption policy. Paged allocators reduce but do not eliminate waste; whether the engine recomputes or swaps on preemption changes tail latency by an order of magnitude. State which.
3. Prefix caching. If prefix/radix caching is on and the benchmark reuses a system prompt, measured throughput is a cache-hit artifact and will not survive on production traffic with diverse prefixes. Report cache hit rate.
4. Whether weights are quantized and whether the quantization is memory-only or also compute. AWQ/GPTQ int4 cuts the weight read to ~4.5 GB and roughly quarters the bandwidth floor, but dequantization overhead and accuracy loss must be reported together.
5. Peak vs steady state. Fragmentation grows over hours; a 60-second benchmark cannot support an OOM-free claim.

Concrete mechanism. Because decode is a bandwidth-bound weight sweep, throughput per GPU is proportional to achievable batch size, and batch size is a pure function of free KV bytes divided by per-sequence context bytes. This makes KV capacity, not FLOPs, the controlling resource on 24 GB cards.

Boundary condition. The model above assumes no CPU offload. If KV or weights are offloaded to host memory over PCIe Gen4 (~25 GB/s effective, ~26x slower than HBM), the bandwidth floor per step rises by the offloaded fraction, and the decode step becomes PCIe-bound instead. Offload claims must state exactly which tensors moved.

Falsifiable prediction. Raise max_model_len from 4k to 8k with everything else fixed: maximum concurrent sequences should fall by roughly 2x and preemption count should become nonzero at the previously stable QPS.

Evidence to demand. Engine memory profiler output, running counters for cache usage/preemptions/swaps, torch.cuda.memory_summary at steady state, and an >=2 hour soak showing no monotonic growth in reserved-but-unallocated memory.

Rollback gate. If steady-state KV utilization exceeds ~90% or preemptions exceed 0.1% of requests, reduce max_num_seqs or max_model_len and revert; do not ship a config whose headroom depends on the benchmark's prompt distribution.

corrected_answer:
Assumptions frame: single-node or 2-node A30-class serving (24 GB HBM2, ~933 GB/s theoretical HBM bandwidth, no NVLink between A30 pairs on this host, PCIe Gen4 x16 ~25 GB/s effective host-device), dense ~9B decoder in bf16 (~18 GB weights), paged KV cache, continuous batching.

Assumptions that must be stated before any decode performance claim (variant: multi-GPU and disaggregation claims).

1. Parallelism layout. TP degree, PP degree, and (for MoE) EP degree, plus which dimension crosses which link. Decode is latency-sensitive and collective-heavy, so the mapping of TP groups onto NVLink vs PCIe vs network dominates the result.
2. Interconnect. nvidia-smi topo -m output, whether GPUDirect RDMA is actually active (not merely compiled in), NIC count and speed, and whether the RoCE fabric has PFC/ECN configured. Claiming RDMA benefit without showing GDR counters moving is not evidence.
3. Whether prefill and decode are colocated or disaggregated. Disaggregated serving (the Mooncake / NVIDIA Dynamo style split) moves KV from prefill workers to decode workers; the claim must state the KV transfer path, transfer size, and whether it overlaps with compute.
4. Scheduler policy across replicas: KV-aware routing vs round robin. A prefix-aware router changes measured throughput far more than kernel-level tuning.
5. Batch composition per worker, since decode workers in a disaggregated setup see a very different (pure-decode, high-B) profile than colocated workers.

Concrete mechanism. In disaggregation, per request the prefill worker must ship the full KV for the prompt: at ~1.6 MB/token, a 2k-token prompt is ~3.2 GB. Over a 200 Gb/s RoCE link at ~80% efficiency (~20 GB/s) that is ~160 ms of transfer, which must be hidden behind layer-by-layer streaming or it simply relocates TTFT rather than reducing it. Over PCIe-only host staging it is far worse. This is why real systems stream KV per layer as it is produced and why GDR (NIC to GPU HBM, bypassing host bounce buffers) matters.

Boundary condition. Disaggregation pays off only when the KV transfer time per request is smaller than the prefill-induced decode stall it removes, i.e. roughly when prompt length is large, output length is long, and the fabric is fast enough that transfer overlaps compute. On a 2-node A30 setup without a high-speed RDMA fabric, the condition typically fails and colocated chunked prefill is the better choice.

Falsifiable prediction. If GDR is genuinely active, host bounce-buffer copies vanish from the Nsight trace and per-transfer latency for a 3.2 GB KV blob drops by more than 30% versus the staged path.

Evidence to demand. nvidia-smi topo -m, ibdev2netdev, perftest (ib_write_bw) numbers between the actual GPU-affine NICs, NCCL_DEBUG=INFO showing NET/IB with GDRDMA enabled, per-layer KV transfer timings, and end-to-end TTFT/ITL distributions for colocated vs disaggregated under identical load.

Rollback gate. Disaggregation ships only if p99 TTFT improves >=20% at the target QPS with no ITL regression; otherwise revert to colocated with chunked prefill.

source_assistant: Decode generates one or a few tokens per step and repeatedly reads model weights and KV state; it is often sensitive to memory bandwidth and scheduling.
corrected_answer:
Assumptions frame: single-node or 2-node A30-class serving (24 GB HBM2, ~933 GB/s theoretical HBM bandwidth, no NVLink between A30 pairs on this host, PCIe Gen4 x16 ~25 GB/s effective host-device), dense ~9B decoder in bf16 (~18 GB weights), paged KV cache, continuous batching.

Assumptions that must be stated before any decode performance claim (variant: comparison and benchmarking hygiene).

1. Both sides of the comparison must be tuned. Comparing engine X default flags against engine Y hand-tuned flags is the most common invalid decode benchmark. State the tuning budget applied to each.
2. Identical model artifact, identical tokenizer, identical quantization, identical max_model_len, identical sampling parameters, identical output-length control. If one system stops at EOS and the other is forced to max_tokens, the tok/s numbers are incomparable.
3. Identical hardware and clocks. Report nvidia-smi -q clock throttle reasons; A30 in a dense chassis can hit thermal or power caps, which silently changes decode step time by 10-20%.
4. Statistical treatment. At least 3 independent runs, report median and dispersion, and state the discard warmup window. A single run with a mean is not a result.
5. Correctness gate. A decode speedup with unreported output-quality change is not a speedup. Pair every performance run with a fixed-seed greedy generation diff or a small task-accuracy check.

Concrete mechanism. Decode step time is dominated by the weight sweep: ~18 GB per step for a bf16 9B, ~28 ms at ~650 GB/s achieved. Most engine-level "wins" therefore come from raising achieved batch size (better scheduling, paged KV, prefix caching) or shrinking bytes moved (quantization, GQA, fp8 KV), not from faster math. A benchmark that does not report achieved batch size and cache hit rate cannot attribute its own result.

Boundary condition. This attribution holds only in the memory-bound regime. Under very large batch with short contexts, decode GEMMs regain arithmetic intensity and the workload can become compute-bound, at which point tensor-core utilization and precision matter more than bandwidth. State which regime the measurement sits in by reporting achieved bandwidth versus achieved FLOP/s.

Falsifiable prediction. Compute achieved bytes/s from the model size and measured step time. If it is within roughly 60-75% of device peak HBM bandwidth, the run is bandwidth-bound and any claimed compute-side optimization should show near-zero effect; that is a direct test of the causal story.

Evidence to demand. Full launch commands for both systems, container digests, driver/CUDA/NCCL versions, raw latency CSVs, DCGM samples for SM occupancy and HBM bandwidth, throttle-reason dumps, and the correctness-check output.

Rollback gate. Do not adopt the winning configuration unless the advantage reproduces on a second, independently provisioned host and survives a 2-hour soak with stable p99 and zero preemption growth; otherwise treat the result as environment-specific and revert.

source_user: Explain how decode changes between training and inference. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Decode generates one or a few tokens per step and repeatedly reads model weights and KV state; it is often sensitive to memory bandwidth and scheduling.
corrected_answer:
Assumptions frame: single-node or 2-node A30-class serving (24 GB HBM2, ~933 GB/s theoretical HBM bandwidth, no NVLink between A30 pairs on this host, PCIe Gen4 x16 ~25 GB/s effective host-device), dense ~9B decoder in bf16 (~18 GB weights), paged KV cache, continuous batching.

How decode differs between training and inference (variant: parallelism and compute shape).

Training. Every step is a full forward and backward over a batch of complete sequences with teacher forcing. All positions are processed in parallel, so the attention and MLP kernels are large GEMMs with high arithmetic intensity; the step is compute-bound and tensor cores are the limiting resource. There is no autoregressive dependency inside a sequence because the targets are known, and causal masking gives the same result as sequential generation.

Inference decode. Tokens are produced one step at a time and each step depends on the previous token, so the sequence dimension collapses to 1. The same weight matrices are now multiplied by a B x 1 x hidden activation: GEMM degenerates to GEMV, arithmetic intensity falls to roughly 2 FLOP/byte, and the step becomes memory-bandwidth-bound. The only way to recover intensity is batching across independent requests.

Concrete mechanism. In training with sequence length 2048 and micro-batch 4, one weight read amortizes over 8192 token-positions. In decode with batch 8, the same weight read amortizes over 8 token-positions, roughly a 1000x drop in reuse. That single ratio explains why an A30 that sustains high TFLOP/s in training sits at a few percent of peak FLOP/s during decode while running near its bandwidth roofline.

Boundary condition. The picture inverts if batch size grows very large or if speculative decoding verifies k>1 draft tokens per step: verifying 4 draft tokens restores 4x sequence parallelism per weight read and moves the step back toward compute-bound, but only when the draft acceptance rate is high enough that the extra work is not wasted. State the measured acceptance rate before claiming a speedup.

Second consequence: parallelism strategy differs. Training tolerates pipeline parallelism because microbatches fill the bubble; decode does not, since there is exactly one token in flight per sequence and PP bubbles appear directly in ITL. Training also uses ZeRO/FSDP sharding of optimizer and gradient state, which has no analogue in decode; decode instead shards weights via TP and pays collective latency per layer.

Falsifiable prediction. Profile one training step and one decode step on the same model and host: training should show >40% tensor-core utilization with modest HBM bandwidth, decode should show <10% tensor-core utilization with HBM bandwidth near 60-75% of peak. If decode instead shows high SM utilization, the deployment is misconfigured (for example unnecessary recomputation or an unfused sampling path).

Evidence required. Nsight Compute or DCGM samples for both phases, engine and trainer configs, measured acceptance rate if speculative decoding is on.

Rollback gate. If a change intended to help decode raises training-side memory or destabilizes loss curves in a shared codebase, revert; do not couple serving optimizations to trainer defaults.

source_user: Explain how decode changes between training and inference. Case variant 2: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Decode generates one or a few tokens per step and repeatedly reads model weights and KV state; it is often sensitive to memory bandwidth and scheduling.
corrected_answer:
Assumptions frame: single-node or 2-node A30-class serving (24 GB HBM2, ~933 GB/s theoretical HBM bandwidth, no NVLink between A30 pairs on this host, PCIe Gen4 x16 ~25 GB/s effective host-device), dense ~9B decoder in bf16 (~18 GB weights), paged KV cache, continuous batching.

How decode differs between training and inference (variant: memory and state).

Training memory is dominated by activations, gradients, and optimizer state. For a 9B model in mixed precision with Adam, parameters plus gradients plus two moments plus an fp32 master copy is roughly 16 bytes per parameter, about 144 GB, which is why full fine-tuning needs sharding (FSDP/ZeRO-3) or many GPUs; activation memory scales with batch x sequence x layers and is usually traded against recomputation.

Inference decode memory is dominated by weights plus KV cache. There are no gradients, no optimizer state, and activations are transient and tiny (one token per sequence). For the same 9B in bf16 that is ~18 GB of weights plus a KV cache whose size is the actual scaling variable.

Concrete mechanism. KV bytes per token = 2 (K and V) * n_kv_heads * head_dim * dtype_bytes * n_layers. With 8 KV heads, head_dim 128, bf16, 40 layers this is ~1.6 MB per token. On a 24 GB A30 holding 18 GB of weights, usable KV after activation and allocator overhead is often under 4 GB, i.e. roughly 2500 total cached tokens across all concurrent sequences. Serving capacity is therefore set by a linear KV budget, whereas training capacity is set by a mostly fixed optimizer-state budget plus a batch-dependent activation term.

Second structural difference: state persistence. Training state is ephemeral within a step and checkpointed periodically; decode state (the KV cache) is per-request, long-lived across many steps, and must be managed with a paged allocator, evicted, recomputed, or migrated between workers. This is precisely the problem that KV-store designs such as Mooncake address by treating KV as a first-class, transferable, cacheable object rather than an engine-internal buffer.

Boundary condition. The "no optimizer state" simplification fails for online or continual post-training and for RLHF-style loops, where a generation phase and a training phase share the same GPUs. There the two memory models collide and you must either time-slice with full engine teardown or dedicate separate GPU pools; attempting to hold both resident on a 24 GB card for a 9B model will OOM.

Falsifiable prediction. Halving KV dtype to fp8 (where supported) or halving max_model_len should roughly double the maximum concurrent sequences at fixed weights, while leaving per-step latency at low batch essentially unchanged, because the weight-read term is untouched.

Evidence required. Engine KV-usage and preemption counters, memory profiler output for both phases, and a fixed-seed quality check when changing KV precision.

Rollback gate. Revert any KV precision change that moves a held-out task metric by more than the pre-agreed tolerance, regardless of the throughput gain.

source_user: Explain how decode changes between training and inference. Case variant 3: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Decode generates one or a few tokens per step and repeatedly reads model weights and KV state; it is often sensitive to memory bandwidth and scheduling.
corrected_answer:
Assumptions frame: single-node or 2-node A30-class serving (24 GB HBM2, ~933 GB/s theoretical HBM bandwidth, no NVLink between A30 pairs on this host, PCIe Gen4 x16 ~25 GB/s effective host-device), dense ~9B decoder in bf16 (~18 GB weights), paged KV cache, continuous batching.

How decode differs between training and inference (variant: collectives and interconnect).

Training collectives are large and bandwidth-bound. Gradient all-reduce or FSDP reduce-scatter/all-gather moves parameter-sized buffers (gigabytes) once per step, and NCCL can pipeline them into large chunks that reach a high fraction of link bandwidth. They also overlap with backward compute, so latency is partly hidden.

Decode collectives are small and latency-bound. With tensor parallelism, every transformer layer needs an all-reduce of the activation tensor, whose size is batch * hidden_size * 2 bytes. At batch 8 and hidden 4096 that is 64 KB per collective, and with ~40 layers and two collectives per layer that is ~80 tiny collectives per token. At this size NCCL is dominated by fixed per-call overhead and link latency, not bandwidth, and there is nothing to overlap with because the next layer depends on the reduced result.

Concrete mechanism. On a host where A30s are connected only through PCIe Gen4 and the CPU root complex (no NVLink on this configuration), a small all-reduce costs on the order of tens of microseconds; 80 of them per token adds several milliseconds to ITL. Meanwhile TP=2 only saves half of the ~28 ms weight-read time. Whether TP helps is a direct comparison of those two quantities, and it must be measured, not assumed.

Boundary condition. The conclusion flips with NVLink or NVSwitch, where small-message all-reduce latency is several times lower, and flips again in multi-node settings where TP should never cross the node boundary; across nodes you use pipeline or data parallelism and, for disaggregated serving, explicit KV transfer over RDMA/RoCE with GPUDirect RDMA so the NIC writes directly into GPU HBM instead of bouncing through host memory.

Additional difference: fault semantics. A training job can checkpoint and restart on a NCCL failure with bounded lost work. A decode replica that loses a collective peer drops live requests; therefore serving TP groups should be kept small, kept inside a node, and placed behind a router that can drain and re-route rather than relying on job-level restart.

Falsifiable prediction. Run an NCCL all-reduce microbenchmark at 64 KB and at 256 MB on this topology. If the 64 KB latency times 80 exceeds half of the measured single-GPU decode step time, TP=2 will not improve ITL at that batch size. This is directly testable before touching the serving stack.

How decode differs between training and inference (variant: scheduling and batching).

Training batching is static and offline. The global batch is chosen up front, sequences are packed or padded to a fixed length, and every microbatch takes essentially the same time. Determinism and gradient-noise properties matter; latency does not.

Decode batching is dynamic and online. Requests arrive at unpredictable times with unpredictable output lengths, and a sequence leaves the batch when it emits EOS. Static batching therefore wastes most of the GPU: the whole batch is held until the longest generation finishes. Continuous (iteration-level) batching fixes this by admitting and retiring sequences at every decode step, which is the single largest throughput lever in serving and has no counterpart in training.

Concrete mechanism. Because one decode step reads all ~18 GB of weights regardless of how many sequences participate, adding a sequence to an in-flight step is nearly free until KV traffic becomes comparable to the weight read. Continuous batching exploits exactly this: it keeps the occupancy of that fixed-cost weight sweep as high as the KV budget allows. Throughput is therefore governed by admission control, not by kernel speed.

Second difference: interference. Prefill of a newly admitted long prompt is compute-heavy and, if run as one monolithic step, stalls every in-flight decoder for tens to hundreds of milliseconds, producing ITL spikes. Chunked prefill slices it into token-budgeted pieces interleaved with decode, trading a small aggregate throughput loss for much tighter ITL tails. Training has no analogous head-of-line blocking problem.

Boundary condition. Continuous batching helps only while KV capacity allows real concurrency. On a 24 GB A30 holding a bf16 9B, usable KV is often under 4 GB (~2500 tokens at ~1.6 MB/token), so at 4k contexts the achievable concurrency is very low and the scheduler spends its time preempting rather than batching. In that regime the correct fix is quantized weights or fp8/shorter KV, not scheduler tuning.

Assumptions frame: single-node or 2-node A30-class serving (24 GB HBM2, ~933 GB/s theoretical HBM bandwidth, no NVLink between A30 pairs on this host, PCIe Gen4 x16 ~25 GB/s effective host-device), dense ~9B decoder in bf16 (~18 GB weights), paged KV cache, continuous batching.

How decode differs between training and inference (variant: numerics, determinism, and correctness).

Training tolerates and even benefits from stochasticity: dropout, data shuffling, non-deterministic reduction order in all-reduce, and TF32/bf16 accumulation all average out over many steps, and the success criterion is an aggregate loss or eval metric. Bitwise reproducibility is usually sacrificed for throughput.

Decode is a sequential amplifier of numerical difference. One token differing at an argmax boundary changes the entire downstream continuation, so a numerically tiny discrepancy becomes a fully different output. This changes what "correct" means and what must be controlled.

Concrete mechanism. Batch size changes the reduction order and kernel selection inside the same GEMM, so the logits for a given sequence are not bitwise identical at batch 1 and batch 16. Near-tied top-2 logits then flip, and with greedy sampling the outputs diverge. This is why serving systems cannot promise bitwise-stable generations under continuous batching, and why any regression test that string-matches generated text will be flaky by construction.

Boundary condition. The divergence only becomes visible when the top-2 logit gap is comparable to the accumulated numerical error (roughly 1e-2 to 1e-3 in bf16). For confidently predicted tokens outputs stay stable; for uncertain positions they will not. Therefore a decode correctness check should assert on distributional or task-level metrics with a tolerance band, or on top-1 agreement rate over many samples, not on exact string equality.

Second difference: quantization risk profile. Post-training weight quantization (AWQ/GPTQ int4) is cheap and often near-lossless in perplexity, yet can degrade long-horizon behaviors such as tool-call argument formatting or code syntax far more than perplexity suggests, because errors compound over hundreds of sequential steps. Perplexity is not an adequate acceptance test for decode-side quantization.

Falsifiable prediction. Run the same fixed prompt set with greedy sampling at batch 1 and at batch 16 on identical weights. Expect a nonzero but small top-1 divergence rate (typically well under a few percent of tokens) concentrated at low-margin positions; if divergence is large or uniformly distributed, suspect a real bug such as an incorrect attention mask, mispaged KV blocks, or a bad quantization kernel rather than benign nondeterminism.

Evidence required. Paired generations at multiple batch sizes with fixed seeds, per-token top-1 margin distributions, and a task-level eval (for example tool-call schema validity and code execution pass rate) run before and after any precision change.

Rollback gate. Revert any precision or kernel change whose task-level metric regresses beyond the agreed tolerance, and never accept a decode-side quantization on perplexity evidence alone.
